title: Tiered SLO Grace Period and Capacity Broker Runbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This runbook describes Redwood Inference’s policy and operational play for applying short-term, tiered SLO grace windows and an automated Capacity Broker when services approach or exceed error-budget and capacity friction thresholds. The intent is to preserve customer-facing availability while preserving long-term SLO discipline and ownership.

Scope

Applies to: all user-facing model-serving services (hosted API, dedicated frontends, and routing proxies).
Excludes: internal-only tooling (CI jobs, analytics pipelines) unless they directly affect production request surfaces.

Why this exists

As traffic patterns fluctuate (batch jobs, large model rollouts, experiments) SLO violations can cascade. A short, structured grace period plus a Capacity Broker that orchestrates temporary prioritized capacity and traffic shaping reduces the blast radius and buys time to remediate root cause, while keeping customers’ critical requests online.

Key concepts

- Tiered SLO Grace Window: a conservative, time-boxed pause on automated punitive actions for specific SLO classes to allow controlled mitigation steps. Three tiers: P0 (no grace), P1 (10–30 min), P2 (1–4 hours).
- Capacity Broker: a control-plane component that enforces routing priorities, temporary capacity reservations, priority queuing, and preemption policies across GPU pools and regions.
- Error-Budget States: Normal, At-Risk, Exhausted — driven by rolling 7d SLO burn and 24h acceleration signal.

Ownership and roles

- SRE Oncall: executes runbook, communicates, triggers Capacity Broker if required.
- Service Owner: leads investigation and remediation; coordinates rollouts and model fallbacks.
- Platform Engineering: owns Capacity Broker automation and capacity policy templates.
- Product/Support: customer comms for impacted paid customers.

Trigger signals and thresholds

Primary signals (examples):
- 7d rolling availability burn rate > 60% of error budget -> At-Risk
- 24h burn acceleration (burn rate last 2h / average previous 24h) > 3x -> Immediate review
- P50 latency > SLO * 1.5 for 5 minutes AND P95 latency > SLO * 1.25 -> traffic shaping candidate
- GPU utilization > 85% in a region + queue depth growth > 25% in 10 minutes -> capacity broker invocation candidate

Decision matrix (human-readable)

| Condition | Immediate action | Grace Tier | Broker action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| P0 service outage (total unavailability) | Pager to SRE & SE | N/A | Emergency preemption and multi-region failover |
| Error budget exhausted for business-critical route | Notify owners + evaluate fallback | P0 | Reserve capacity from low-priority pools, elevate queue priority |
| Burst causing elevated latency but partial success | Monitor + advisory | P1 (10–30m) | Prioritized queuing, temporary burst pool attach |
| Sustained slow burn trending to exhaustion | Prep mitigations | P2 (1–4h) | Schedule capacity transfers and scheduled throttle windows |

Runbook — step-by-step

1) Detection & Triage (SRE Oncall)
   - Confirm alerts and correlated telemetry (SLO dashboard, per-route latency, GPU pool utilization, queue depth).
   - Run quick queries: 
     - curl -s https://telemetry.redwood.internal/api/now?service=<svc>&window=2m | jq '.slo.burn'
     - kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=<svc> -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}'
   - Classify impact (P0/P1/P2) and choose Grace Tier.

2) Initial containment (0–15 minutes)
   - If P0: trigger emergency fallback (route to replica region or model variant) and escalate to SEs.
   - If P1/P2: enable Tiered Grace Window for the affected route using the SLO policy API:

     POST /platform/slo-policy/activate
     {
       "service": "<svc>",
       "grace_tier": "P1",
       "duration_minutes": 20,
       "reason": "traffic_burst_{YYYYMMDDHHmm}"
     }

   - The policy API will: (a) pause automatic punitive throttles for the route, (b) emit an auditable event, (c) notify Platform Engineering.

3) Capacity Broker invocation (15–60 minutes)
   - If capacity signals persist, call Capacity Broker CLI to create a temporary reservation:

     redwood-capacity broker reserve --service <svc> --priority high --gpu-kind a100-80gb --region us-west1 --minutes 120 --preemptible-allowed true

   - Broker will attempt these actions in order (configurable):
     1. Attach burst pool (pre-warmed GPUs).
     2. Rebalance less-critical tenant jobs to other regions/pools.
     3. Elevate request queue priority for the service.
     4. If all else fails, preempt non-critical low-priority pods with 15m termination window.

4) Traffic shaping and graceful degradation (concurrent)
   - Apply per-route soft-fallbacks: shorter generation length limits, episodic response sampling, explicit 429 retry-after headers for low-priority customers. Example config snippet: 

     routes:
       - name: /v1/generate
         priority_profile: high
         fallback: "+short_gen,partial_response"
         throttle_policy: \"adaptive\"

   - Notify customer-facing teams for targeted comms if paid customers are impacted.

5) Escalation and remediation (60–240 minutes)
   - Service owner performs root cause (model regression, kernel contention, infra failure).
   - If remediation requires rollback or model pinning, follow the Model Rollout rollback checklist (link in related_pages).
   - If Capacity Broker reservation is insufficient, schedule emergency capacity reallocation with Platform Engineering.

6) Grace end and enforcement (post-window)
   - At Grace expiration, the policy controller will automatically: re-enable throttles, decrement temporary reservations, and publish a compliance event.
   - If the service remains in an unhealthy state, move to enforcement: automatic rate limits and customer-facing throttles are restored.

Automation, observability and telemetry requirements

Minimum telemetry items (must be present for broker to act automatically):
- Per-route 1m and 5m SLO burn, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), error classification (4xx/5xx/model-failures).
- GPU pool utilization and per-node queue depth.
- Capacity Broker action logs (audit trail).
- Grace policy events with start/end timestamps and operator id.

SLO policy schema (example YAML)

- service: com.redwood.svc.generate
  slo_set:
    - name: availability
      target: 99.5
      window_days: 7
  grace_policies:
    - tier: P1
      duration_minutes: 20
      allowed_actions: [reserve_capacity, elevate_priority, suspend_backpressure]

Safety and guardrails

- Grace windows are explicit and auditable. No manual, indefinite grace. Max single grace for a route: 4 hours in a 30-day window.
- Capacity Broker must respect multi-tenant fairness labels: reserved capacity is isolated to the extent that it cannot starve critical system services.
- All preemption must respect a 15-minute drain window and Post-Preempt hooks must trigger automated requeue or job resumption logic.

Customer communication play

- If paid customers are in the impacted cohort, Customer Support & AE are notified at the At-Risk threshold.
- Draft notice template (50–200 chars):
  \"We are experiencing elevated latency for <svc> and have applied short-term mitigations to preserve availability. We will follow up with impact and timeline.\"

Post-incident review and continuous improvement

- For any invocation of the Capacity Broker that lasted > 30 minutes or involved preemption, require a focused incident review within 5 business days.
- Incident review must cover:
  - Why the grace was needed (root cause summary).
  - Broker actions executed and time-to-attach/reserve.
  - Cost impact estimate (reserved minutes, preemptions).
  - Suggested permanent fixes (capacity increases, model quantization, query shape changes).

Metrics to track (SRE program)

- Number of grace activations per service per month (target <= 2 for business-critical routes).
- Mean time to attach capacity (target < 10 minutes for pre-warmed pools).
- Post-grace violation rate (percent of grace windows followed by enforcement within 24h).
- Cost delta attributable to broker actions (monthly).

Operational checklist (quick reference)

- Confirm alert -> classify P-tier -> activate grace policy -> call capacity broker -> apply traffic shaping -> track uptime and burn -> expire grace and re-evaluate -> open review if >30m.

Appendix A — Example CLI snippets

Reserve capacity (programmatic):

curl -X POST https://platform.redwood.internal/v1/broker/reserve -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"service":"com.redwood.svc.generate","gpu_kind":"a100-80gb","minutes":120,"priority":"high"}'

Cancel reservation:

redwood-capacity broker cancel --id <reservation-id>

Appendix B — Audit event example (JSON string for logs)

{
  "event_type": "grace_policy.activate",
  "service": "com.redwood.svc.generate",
  "tier": "P1",
  "start_ts": "2027-02-15T02:13:00Z",
  "initiated_by": "oncall-aisha@redwood.internal",
  "reason": "scheduled-batch-burst"
}
